parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State what is meant by the work done by a force.

markscheme_points.text: product of force and displacement in direction of force

hints: Hint 1: Think about what must happen for a force to transfer energy - what two things about the motion relative to the force really matter?
parts.proper_answer: Work done by a force is the product of the force and the displacement in the direction of the force.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What work really means**
Think of pushing a box along the floor. You only transfer energy when the box actually moves, and only the part of your push along the movement counts. If you push forward but it moves forward, you do work. If you carry it sideways, that sideways force does no work.

Step 2: **The precise definition**
So we say $$W = F \times d$$ where $d$ is the displacement measured in the direction of the force $F$. Both must be in the same direction for full work to be done.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
A block of mass $m$ is raised vertically at constant speed. The vertical height gained by the block is $\Delta h$, as shown in Fig. 3.1.

{{figure:figure_3_1}}

Fig. 3.1

Derive an expression, in terms of $m$ and $\Delta h$, for the change in gravitational potential energy $\Delta E_{\text{P}}$ of the block. State the meaning of any other symbols you use.

markscheme_points.text: weight/force = mg, and g identified as acceleration of free fall
ΔEp identified as work (done by lifting force/weight), and so = mg × Δh

hints: Hint 1: The block moves at constant speed upward, so what must the lifting force balance, and how is that force linked to mass $m$?
Hint 2: Now link the energy gained to the work done by that lifting force over distance $\Delta h$, remembering to define $g$.
parts.proper_answer: $\Delta E_P = mg\Delta h$, where $m$ is mass, $g$ is acceleration of free fall and $\Delta h$ is vertical height gained. Work done by lifting force = force $\times$ distance = $mg\Delta h$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Force needed to lift at constant speed**
Constant speed means no resultant force, so the upward lifting force must exactly balance the weight pulling down. Weight is mass times gravitational field strength: $$W = mg$$ where $g$ is the acceleration of free fall, about $9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.

Step 2: **Work becomes stored energy**
The work done by the lifting force is force times vertical displacement: $$W = \text{force} \times \Delta h = mg \times \Delta h$$ This work is not lost, it is stored as gravitational potential energy of the block. So $$\Delta E_P = mg\Delta h$$

parts.label: (c)
parts.part_stem: An electric motor has an input power of $900 \text{ W}$. The motor takes $1.0$ minute to lift a load of weight $240 \text{ N}$ at constant speed through a vertical height of $150 \text{ m}$. Resistive forces are negligible.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.text: Show that the work done by the motor on the load in $1.0$ minute is $36 \text{ kJ}$.
hints: Hint 1: Identify which given value already is the force in the direction of motion, and which is the distance moved that way.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Apply work directly**
The weight $240 \text{ N}$ is already the force opposing the lift, and $150 \text{ m}$ is the displacement in that direction. So: $$W = F \times d = 240 \times 150$$ $$W = 36000 \text{ J} = 36 \text{ kJ}$$ This is the useful work done on the load, which equals its gain in potential energy.

enrichment.label: (c)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Identify which given value already is the force in the direction of motion, and which is the distance moved that way.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Apply work directly**
The weight $240 \text{ N}$ is already the force opposing the lift, and $150 \text{ m}$ is the displacement in that direction. So: $$W = F \times d = 240 \times 150$$ $$W = 36000 \text{ J} = 36 \text{ kJ}$$ This is the useful work done on the load, which equals its gain in potential energy.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: Determine the useful output power of the motor.
hints: Hint 1: Power tells you how fast work is done, so think about which two quantities from (c)(i) and the time you need to combine.
Hint 2: Check your time units are in seconds before dividing to get watts.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall power**
Power is the rate of doing work: $$P = \frac{W}{t}$$

Step 2: **Insert values in SI units**
Time $t = 1.0 \text{ minute} = 60 \text{ s}$ and $W = 36000 \text{ J}$: $$P = \frac{36000}{60} = 600 \text{ W}$$ This is the useful output power delivered to the load.

parts.label: (c)(iii)
parts.text: Use your answer in (c)(ii) to determine the efficiency of the motor.

markscheme_points.text: efficiency = useful output power / total input power

hints: Hint 1: Efficiency compares what you get out usefully to what you put in - which power from (c)(ii) is useful and what is the total input?
Hint 2: Set up the ratio of those two powers, keeping both in watts so units cancel.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Efficiency idea**
No motor is perfect. Efficiency is the fraction that is useful: $$\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output power}}{\text{total input power}}$$

Step 2: **Calculate**
Useful output $= 600 \text{ W}$, input $= 900 \text{ W}$: $$\text{efficiency} = \frac{600}{900} = 0.67$$ This can also be written as $67\%$. It has no unit.

parts.label: (c)(iv)
parts.text:
Some of the power wasted in the motor is dissipated by the resistance of its coil. This dissipated power is $280 \text{ W}$.

The coil of the motor is made from wire of total length $23 \text{ m}$. The wire has a cross-sectional area of $2.6 \times 10^{-8} \text{ m}^2$ and is made from metal of resistivity $1.7 \times 10^{-8} \Omega \text{ m}$.

Calculate the current in the coil.

markscheme_points.text: P = I²R and R = ρL / A

hints: Hint 1: The 280 W is heating in the coil, so think about which electrical power law links power to current and resistance.
Hint 2: You do not know $R$ yet, but you have length, area and resistivity - think how those give resistance.
Hint 3: Combine the two steps to solve for current, watching the powers of ten carefully.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Two laws to combine**
Heating power in a resistor is $$P = I^2 R$$ and resistance from material properties is $$R = \frac{\rho L}{A}$$ where $\rho$ is resistivity, $L$ is length and $A$ is cross-sectional area.

Step 2: **Find the coil resistance first**
$$R = \frac{(1.7 \times 10^{-8}) \times 23}{2.6 \times 10^{-8}}$$ The $10^{-8}$ cancels: $$R = \frac{1.7 \times 23}{2.6} \approx 15 \text{ }\Omega$$

Step 3: **Solve for current**
Rearrange $P = I^2 R$ to $$I = \sqrt{\frac{P}{R}} = \sqrt{\frac{280}{15.0}}$$ $$I \approx 4.3 \text{ A}$$
